title: Indian Penal Code (IPC) — Overview and Key Provisions
content:
The Indian Penal Code (IPC), enacted in 1860, is the primary criminal code of India. It defines offences and prescribes punishments for criminal acts committed within Indian territory. The IPC was substantially replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) 2023, which came into force on 1 July 2024.

The IPC/BNS covers a wide range of offences including offences against the state, offences against public tranquillity, offences related to religion, offences affecting the human body, offences against property, and offences relating to documents and property marks.

Cheating and fraud are covered under Sections 415–420 of the IPC (now Sections 316–318 of BNS). Section 420 IPC (cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property) is one of the most frequently invoked sections for financial fraud cases. The maximum punishment is up to seven years imprisonment with fine.

Cheating by personation (Section 416 IPC) occurs when a person cheats by pretending to be someone else, including online identity fraud. Online fraud committed using electronic means is also covered under the Information Technology Act 2000, Section 66C (identity theft) and Section 66D (cheating by personation using computer resources), in addition to the IPC.

Theft is defined under Section 378 IPC (Section 303 BNS) as dishonestly taking movable property out of the possession of a person without their consent. Robbery is aggravated theft with force or threat (Section 390 IPC). Extortion is covered under Section 383 IPC.

Criminal breach of trust is defined under Section 405 IPC. It applies when a person entrusted with property dishonestly misappropriates or converts it. This is relevant in employer-employee relationships where employees handle funds, and in investment fraud situations.

First Information Report (FIR): Any cognisable offence must be reported to the police who are obligated to register a FIR under Section 154 CrPC (now Section 173 BNSS). If the police refuse to register an FIR, the complainant may approach the Superintendent of Police or file a complaint directly before a Magistrate under Section 156(3) CrPC.

The National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (www.cybercrime.gov.in) allows victims of online fraud, cybercrime, and financial fraud to file complaints online. Complaints are forwarded to the relevant state police.

For financial fraud involving banks or payment systems, complaints should also be filed with the bank's grievance officer, and if unresolved, with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Ombudsman.

Limitation period: Criminal complaints generally have no hard time bar for serious offences, but delay in reporting weakens the case. For minor offences, Sections 467–473 CrPC prescribe limitation periods.
